title: Black Holes
summary: What black holes are, how they form when giant stars collapse, and how scientists find and even photograph something that gives off no light.
poll: Black holes are the most interesting things in space.

versions.title: Black Holes
versions.text:
Look up at night. You see stars. But some things in space can not be seen. A black hole is one.

A black hole is a spot in space. Its pull is strong. This pull is called gravity. It pulls on all things. Not even light can escape. So the spot looks black.

How does one form? It starts with a huge star. The star burns for a long time. Then its fuel runs out. The star falls in. It gets squeezed small. Now its pull is huge.

We can not see a black hole. So how do we find one? We watch stars near it. They spin fast. They spin round a spot that looks bare. Gas near it gets hot. It glows.

In 2019, a big team used a telescope link. It was the size of the world. They got the first shot of the dark shape of one.

Do not be scared. Black holes are far from us. Our Sun is too small to be one.

versions.title: Black Holes
versions.text:
Look up at the sky on a clear night. You can see lots of stars. But some things in space can not be seen. A black hole is one of them.

A black hole is a place in space with a very strong pull. This pull is called gravity. Gravity pulls all things in. In a black hole, the pull is so strong that not even light can escape. That is why it looks black.

How does a black hole form? It starts with a huge star. The star shines for a long time. Then it runs out of fuel. The star falls in on itself. It is squeezed into a very small space. Now its pull is very strong.

We can not see a black hole. So how do we find one? We watch the stars near it. They spin fast around a spot that looks empty. Gas near the black hole gets very hot. It glows.

In 2019, a team of scientists linked telescopes around the world. They took the first picture of the dark shape of a black hole.

Do not worry. Black holes are very far from Earth. Our Sun is too small to become one.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Darkest Places in Space
versions.text:
On a clear night, thousands of stars shine above you. Yet some of the strangest things in space cannot be seen at all. A black hole is one of them.

A black hole is a place in space where gravity is very strong. Gravity is the force that pulls things toward each other. It keeps your feet on the ground. It also keeps Earth moving around the Sun. Near a black hole, the pull is so strong that nothing can escape, not even light. Since no light can get out, a black hole looks black.

Most black holes form from giant stars that are much heavier than our Sun. A star like this shines for millions of years. When it runs out of fuel, it falls in on itself. All of its matter is squeezed into a tiny space, which makes its pull very strong.

We cannot see a black hole, so how do scientists find one? They watch the stars near it. Those stars race around a spot that looks empty. Gas pulled toward a black hole also swirls fast and gets so hot that it glows.

In 2019, scientists linked telescopes from around the world. Working as one team, they took the first picture of the dark shape of a black hole.

You do not need to worry. Black holes are very far from Earth. Our Sun is too small to ever become one.

versions.title: Black Holes: Where Light Cannot Escape
versions.text:
On a clear night, thousands of stars shine above you. Yet some of the most amazing things in space are impossible to see. Black holes are among them.

A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape, not even light. Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward each other. It holds you on the ground and keeps Earth in orbit around the Sun. Because no light can get out of a black hole, it looks completely black.

Most black holes form from massive stars, which are about twenty times heavier than our Sun or more. Such a star shines for millions of years. When it runs out of fuel, it can no longer hold itself up, and it begins to collapse. Its matter is squeezed into a very small space, so its gravity becomes extremely strong.

The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon. Anything that crosses this edge can never come back out.

Scientists cannot see a black hole, so they look for clues. They watch stars that orbit a spot that seems empty. They also see gas that swirls toward a black hole and gets so hot that it glows.

At the center of our galaxy, the Milky Way, there is a giant black hole. It holds about four million times as much matter as the Sun.

In 2019, scientists linked telescopes around the world and took the first picture of the dark shadow of a black hole in another galaxy.

There is no need to worry. Black holes are very far from Earth, and our Sun is too small to ever become one.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Universe's Hidden Giants
versions.text:
On a clear night, thousands of stars glitter overhead, yet some of the most fascinating objects in the universe cannot be observed directly, because they emit no light whatsoever. These hidden giants are black holes.

A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so powerful that nothing can escape from it, not even light. Gravity is the invisible force that pulls objects toward one another; it holds you on the ground and keeps Earth traveling in orbit around the Sun. Since no light can leave a black hole, it appears completely black against the darkness of space.

Most black holes are created when a massive star, one containing approximately twenty times as much matter as our Sun or more, reaches the end of its life. After shining for millions of years, the star exhausts its fuel and can no longer support its own enormous weight. Its outer layers are blasted into space in a gigantic explosion called a supernova, while its core collapses inward. The remaining matter is crushed into an incredibly small space, which makes the object so dense that its gravity becomes extraordinarily intense.

The boundary surrounding a black hole is called the event horizon. Anything that crosses it, including light, can never return, which is why scientists sometimes describe it as the point of no return.

Because black holes are invisible, astronomers detect them by searching for indirect evidence. They carefully track stars that race in orbit around a region that appears empty, and they observe gas that spirals inward and becomes so hot that it glows brilliantly.

At the center of our galaxy, the Milky Way, lies a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*, which contains approximately four million times as much matter as the Sun.

In 2019, an international team of scientists linked radio telescopes on several continents so that they operated like a single telescope as wide as Earth. Together, they produced the first image of the dark shadow of a black hole, located in a distant galaxy, and in 2022 they released a similar picture of Sagittarius A*.

There is no reason for alarm, however. Black holes are extremely distant from Earth, and our Sun is much too small ever to become one.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Universe's Hidden Giants
versions.text:
On a clear night, thousands of stars glitter overhead, yet some of the most fascinating objects in the universe cannot be observed directly, because they emit no detectable light whatsoever. These concealed giants are black holes, and they rank among the most extreme phenomena that physicists and astronomers have ever investigated.

A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so overwhelming that nothing can escape from it, not even light. Gravity is the invisible force that attracts objects toward one another; it anchors you to the ground and keeps Earth traveling in a predictable orbit around the Sun. Since no light can leave a black hole, it appears completely black against the surrounding darkness of space.

Most black holes originate when a massive star, one containing approximately twenty times as much matter as our Sun or more, approaches the end of its existence. After shining for millions of years, the star exhausts its nuclear fuel and can no longer support its own tremendous weight, so its outer layers are hurled into space in a colossal explosion called a supernova, while its core collapses catastrophically inward. The remaining matter is compressed into an unimaginably small volume, which renders the object so dense that its gravity becomes extraordinarily intense.

The boundary surrounding a black hole is known as the event horizon, and anything that crosses it, including light, can never return, which is why scientists frequently characterize it as the point of no return.

Because black holes are fundamentally invisible, astronomers detect them by assembling indirect evidence. They meticulously track stars that race in orbit around a region that appears empty, and they observe gas that spirals inward, accelerating and heating until it glows brilliantly.

At the center of our galaxy, the Milky Way, lies a supermassive black hole designated Sagittarius A*, which contains approximately four million times as much matter as the Sun.

In 2019, an international collaboration of scientists synchronized radio telescopes on several continents so that they functioned like a single instrument as wide as Earth. Together, they produced the first image of the dark shadow of a black hole, located in a distant galaxy, and in 2022 they published a comparable photograph of Sagittarius A*.

There is no reason for alarm, however. Black holes are tremendously distant from Earth, and our Sun is far too small ever to become one; instead, it will eventually shrink into a dim object called a white dwarf.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Universe's Hidden Giants
versions.text:
On a clear night, thousands of stars glitter overhead, yet some of the most fascinating objects in the universe cannot be observed directly, because they emit no detectable light whatsoever. These concealed giants are black holes, and they rank among the most extreme phenomena that physicists and astronomers have ever investigated, challenging our understanding of space, time, and matter.

A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so overwhelming that nothing can escape from it, not even light. Gravity, the invisible force that attracts objects toward one another, anchors you to the ground and keeps Earth traveling in a predictable orbit around the Sun. Since no light can leave a black hole, it appears completely black against the surrounding darkness of space, an absence rather than a visible object.

Most black holes originate when a massive star, one containing approximately twenty times as much matter as our Sun or more, approaches the conclusion of its existence. After radiating energy for millions of years, the star exhausts its nuclear fuel and can no longer support its own tremendous weight. Its outer layers are hurled into space in a colossal explosion called a supernova, while its core collapses catastrophically inward. The remaining matter is compressed into an unimaginably small volume, which renders the object so extraordinarily dense that its gravitational influence becomes overwhelmingly intense.

The boundary surrounding a black hole is known as the event horizon, and anything that crosses it, including light, can never return, which is why scientists frequently characterize it as the point of no return.

Because black holes are fundamentally invisible, astronomers detect them by assembling indirect evidence. They meticulously track stars that race in orbit around a region that appears empty, and they analyze gas that spirals inward, accelerating and heating until it radiates brilliantly.

At the center of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, astronomers have identified a supermassive black hole designated Sagittarius A*, which contains approximately four million times as much matter as the Sun and powerfully influences the movements of the stars surrounding it.

In 2019, an international collaboration of scientists synchronized radio telescopes on several continents so that they functioned collectively like a single instrument as wide as Earth. Together, they produced the first image of the dark shadow of a black hole, located in a distant galaxy, and in 2022 they published a comparable photograph of Sagittarius A*, confirming predictions that physicists had formulated decades earlier.

There is no reason for alarm, however, because black holes are tremendously distant from Earth, and our Sun is far too small ever to become one; instead, it will eventually contract into a dim, compact object called a white dwarf.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Universe's Hidden Giants
versions.text:
A black hole is a region of space where gravity has become so overwhelmingly dense and powerful that nothing, not even light, can escape its pull once past a certain boundary. These extraordinary objects typically form from the collapse of massive stars, those with at least twenty times the mass of our Sun. When such a star exhausts its nuclear fuel, it can no longer sustain the internal pressure that previously held it together, and its outer layers are violently expelled in an explosion known as a supernova, while its core collapses inward upon itself, compressing into an object of extreme density.

The boundary surrounding a black hole, known as the event horizon, marks the point beyond which nothing can return. Once an object crosses this threshold, escape becomes impossible, regardless of its speed or power. Because black holes emit no light, astronomers cannot detect them directly. Instead, they must rely on indirect evidence, such as observing stars that orbit an invisible companion, or detecting the characteristic glow produced by superheated gas and matter spiraling inexorably into a black hole before disappearing beyond its horizon.

At the center of our own Milky Way galaxy lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole believed to contain the mass of roughly four million Suns compressed into a comparatively small region. In 2019, an international collaboration using the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of linked radio telescopes effectively functioning as a single instrument the size of Earth, produced the first-ever image capturing the shadow cast by a black hole, located in a distant galaxy. This achievement was followed in 2022 by a similarly groundbreaking image, this time of Sagittarius A* itself.

Not every massive star culminates in a black hole, however. Our own Sun, for instance, lacks sufficient mass to ever collapse into one; instead, astronomers predict that it will eventually become a white dwarf, a comparatively modest and far less exotic stellar remnant. The contrast between these two possible fates underscores just how extraordinary and rare black holes truly are among the countless stars that populate the observable universe.

Each new observation gathered by astronomers adds to a growing body of evidence confirming that black holes, however invisible and seemingly abstract, exert measurable and remarkably consistent effects on the matter and light surrounding them, effects precise enough to calculate a black hole's mass and location with considerable confidence.

Such discoveries remind us that even phenomena invisible to direct observation can still be studied rigorously, provided scientists develop sufficiently clever indirect methods of detection.

versions.title: Black Holes: The Universe's Hidden Giants
versions.text:
A black hole constitutes a region of space in which gravitational forces have become so overwhelmingly dense and powerful that nothing whatsoever, not even light itself, can escape beyond a certain threshold. Such extraordinary objects typically originate from the gravitational collapse of exceptionally massive stars, specifically those possessing at least twenty times the mass of our own Sun. When a star of this magnitude eventually exhausts its available nuclear fuel, it becomes incapable of sustaining the internal pressure that had previously counterbalanced its own gravity, and its outer layers are consequently expelled with tremendous violence in an explosive event known as a supernova, while its core simultaneously collapses inward upon itself, compressing into an object of almost unimaginable density.

The boundary encircling a black hole, formally designated the event horizon, demarcates the precise point beyond which return becomes physically impossible; once any object crosses this threshold, no conceivable velocity or propulsive force could permit its escape. Because black holes themselves emit no detectable light, astronomers are unable to observe them directly and must instead rely upon indirect evidence, such as monitoring the orbital motion of visible stars circling an otherwise invisible companion, or detecting the characteristic luminous glow produced as gas and matter spiral inward before vanishing permanently beyond the horizon.

At the very center of our own Milky Way galaxy resides Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole estimated to contain mass equivalent to roughly four million Suns, compressed into a region of comparatively modest spatial extent. In 2019, an international collaboration employing the Event Horizon Telescope, an extensive network of linked radio telescopes functioning collectively as a single instrument effectively the size of Earth, succeeded in producing the first-ever image capturing the shadow cast by a black hole, situated within a distant galaxy. This landmark achievement was subsequently followed in 2022 by an equally groundbreaking image, on this occasion depicting Sagittarius A* itself, a feat that astronomers worldwide had long considered essentially unattainable.

Not every sufficiently massive star, however, culminates its existence as a black hole. Our own Sun, for instance, lacks the requisite mass ever to collapse into such an object; astronomers instead predict that it will eventually become a white dwarf, a comparatively modest and considerably less exotic form of stellar remnant. This contrast between two dramatically different stellar fates underscores precisely how extraordinary, and how statistically rare, black holes truly remain among the vast multitude of stars populating the observable universe.

Each new observation gathered by astronomers studying these phenomena adds incrementally to an expanding body of evidence confirming that black holes, however invisible and conceptually abstract they may initially appear, nonetheless exert measurable and remarkably consistent gravitational effects upon the matter and light surrounding them, effects sufficiently precise to allow astronomers to calculate a given black hole's mass and approximate location with considerable scientific confidence, even in the complete absence of any directly visible signal from the object itself.

questions.why: The article explains that without fuel the star can no longer support its weight and begins to collapse.

wrong.A: The star does not become a planet.
wrong.B: The article does not say the star moves around the Sun.
wrong.C: The star collapses; the article does not say it shines more.

questions.stem: Why might gas near a black hole be easier to spot than the black hole itself?
options: The gas gets so hot that it glows and gives off light.
The gas is much colder than the black hole and the stars.
The gas is closer to Earth than any star.
The gas is the same color as the sky.
questions.why: The article says gas swirling toward a black hole gets so hot it glows. Light from the glowing gas can be seen, but the black hole gives off none.

wrong.B: The article says the gas becomes very hot, not cold.
wrong.C: The article does not say the gas is closer to Earth.
wrong.D: If it matched the sky, it would be harder to spot, not easier.

questions.stem: How is our Sun different from the stars that become black holes?
options: It is much hotter than they are.
It has no gravity at all.
It is much smaller and has far less matter.
It is in a different galaxy.
questions.why: Black holes form from stars about twenty times heavier than the Sun or more, and the article says the Sun is too small to become one.

wrong.A: The article does not compare how hot the stars are.
wrong.B: The article explains that the Sun's gravity keeps Earth in orbit.
wrong.D: The article does not say these stars are in another galaxy.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: By telling the whole life story of one famous scientist from long ago
By listing reasons people should fear space
By comparing two different planets
By telling what they are, how they form, and how they are found
questions.why: The article moves from what a black hole is, to how it forms, to its edge, to the clues scientists use and the first picture.

wrong.A: No single scientist's life story is told.
wrong.B: The article tells readers there is no need to worry.
wrong.C: The article is about black holes, not planets.

MID.prompt: Describe, step by step, how a massive star becomes a black hole. Then explain why scientists must use clues to find black holes.
checklist: I put the steps of how a black hole forms in the right order.
I explained why black holes must be found with clues, using details from the article.
I used at least two key words from the lesson correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: A massive star shines for millions of years, but when it finally runs out of fuel, it can no longer support its own weight and begins to collapse. As it collapses, its matter is crushed into a very small space, which makes its gravity extremely strong and forms a black hole with an event horizon that nothing can cross and return from. Scientists must use clues to find black holes because no light can ever escape them, so instead they watch stars orbiting an area that seems empty or observe gas glowing brightly as it swirls toward the galaxy's hidden center.

keyWords.definition: a giant explosion that happens when a very large star dies
keyWords.example: Long ago, people saw a supernova so bright that it could be seen in the daytime.

keyWords.definition: having a lot of matter packed tightly into a small space
keyWords.example: The forest was so dense that sunlight barely reached the ground.

keyWords.definition: extremely large in mass, millions or billions of times more than the Sun
keyWords.example: Most large galaxies seem to have a supermassive black hole at their center.

keyWords.definition: to discover or notice something that is hard to see
keyWords.example: The smoke alarm can detect even a small amount of smoke.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies stars, planets, and other objects in space
keyWords.example: The astronomer stayed awake all night to measure the comet's path.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Black holes are invisible regions of extreme gravity studied through indirect evidence.
Supernovas are the most common kind of explosion that astronomers have seen in our galaxy.
Radio telescopes will soon allow people to travel to black holes.
The Milky Way is the only galaxy that has a black hole.
questions.why: The article explains what black holes are, how they form, and how astronomers detect and image them even though they give off no light.

wrong.B: Supernovas are part of how black holes form, but the article does not say how common they are.
wrong.C: The telescopes take images; the article never mentions travel.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens during a supernova?
options: The star's core expands outward again and again until it grows into a whole new galaxy.
The star's outer layers are blasted into space while its core collapses.
The star slowly cools into a planet.
Two black holes combine into one supermassive black hole.

wrong.C: The article does not describe stars cooling into planets.
wrong.D: The article does not describe black holes combining.

questions.stem: How did scientists produce the first image of a black hole's shadow?
options: They sent a spacecraft through the event horizon to take a photograph from the inside.
They used one very large mirror in the desert.
They linked radio telescopes on several continents into one Earth-sized telescope.
They waited for a supernova to light up the black hole.

wrong.B: The article describes many linked telescopes, not one mirror.
wrong.D: The image did not depend on a supernova.

questions.stem: The article says the collapsed matter becomes so dense that its gravity is intense. What does dense mean here?
options: Moving at a very high speed
Glowing with a bright light
Spread thinly across space
Packed tightly into a small space

wrong.A: Dense describes how tightly matter is packed, not speed.
wrong.B: Glowing describes the hot gas, not density.
wrong.C: This is the opposite of dense.

questions.stem: Why are astronomers able to detect black holes even though black holes give off no light?
options: Black holes affect the stars and gas around them in ways that can be observed.

Black holes make a sound that radio telescopes hear.
Black holes are always found next to bright planets.

questions.stem: Why do scientists call the event horizon the point of no return?
options: Because it is the place where stars are born
Because anything that crosses it, even light, can never come back out
Because telescopes on Earth are never able to point in that direction of space
Because it marks the end of the Milky Way

wrong.B: The article says the Sun is far too small to become a black hole.
wrong.C: The images came from telescopes on Earth.

HIGH.prompt: Black holes cannot be seen, yet astronomers are confident they exist. Using evidence from the article, explain how scientists know black holes are real and which piece of evidence you find most convincing.
checklist: I explained at least two kinds of evidence astronomers use.
I chose the most convincing evidence and gave a reason.
I used precise vocabulary from the article and organized my answer in clear paragraphs.
HIGH.modelAnswer:
Astronomers rely on indirect evidence to confirm black holes exist, since a black hole itself emits no light at all. One kind of evidence is watching stars orbit around what otherwise looks like empty space, which suggests something supermassive and invisible is pulling on them with its gravity. Another kind is observing gas that becomes extremely dense and hot as it swirls toward a black hole, glowing brightly enough for telescopes to detect.

I find the direct image produced in 2019, when scientists connected telescopes around the world to photograph the dark shadow of a black hole in a distant galaxy, the most convincing evidence of all. Unlike inferring a black hole's presence from the behavior of nearby stars or gas, this image let scientists actually detect the shadow where light disappears, which feels like the closest thing to truly seeing something that is, by definition, impossible to see directly.
